claim_verdicts.evidence: saving/transactions.md > Default transaction behavior: "By default, if the database provider supports transactions, all changes in a single call to SaveChanges are applied in a transaction. If any of the changes fail, then the transaction is rolled back and none of the changes are applied to the database." saving/basic.md NOTE: "For most database providers, SaveChanges is transactional ... the operations are never be left partially applied." Npgsql is a relational provider, so the provider condition holds for this lesson.

modeling/generated-properties.md > Primary keys: "By convention, non-composite primary keys of type short, int, long, or Guid are set up to have values generated for inserted entities if a value isn't provided by the application." PostgreSQL 17 CREATE TABLE: "If BY DEFAULT is selected, then the user-specified value takes precedence" — section 4's "filled in only when `INSERT` supplies no value" is exact here.

claim_verdicts.evidence: change-tracking/miscellaneous.md > `Add` versus `AddAsync`: "Add ... do not normally access the database, since these methods inherently just start tracking entities. However, some forms of value generation _may_ access the database in order to generate a key value. The only value generator that does this and ships with EF Core is HiLoValueGenerator. Using this generator is uncommon; it is never configured by default." orders.id is an identity column (claim 3), not HiLo, so AddAsync touches no database here.

change-tracking/miscellaneous.md > Temporary values: "EF Core creates temporary key values when tracking new entities that will have real key values generated by the database when SaveChanges is called" and "Temporary values are stored in the change tracker and not set onto entity instances directly." explicit-tracking.md: "temporary key values have been generated for each entity. These values are used by EF Core until SaveChanges is called, at which point real key values are read back from the database."

Per-call scope is documented (transactions.md L17, quoted at claim 2), and "Controlling transactions" exists to override it: "The following example shows two SaveChanges operations and a LINQ query being executed in a single transaction." But the same page qualifies the mechanism: AutoTransactionBehavior.WhenNeeded "(default): EF creates a transaction only when needed ... most single SQL statements execute in a transaction implicitly, so EF doesn't create an explicit transaction"; and with a transaction already open, SaveChanges "automatically creates a savepoint" instead.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: By default, one `SaveChangesAsync()` call saves its staged changes all-or-nothing and independently of any other call: a later call cannot undo what an earlier one already saved.

claim_verdicts.evidence: change-tracking/explicit-tracking.md: "the Add methods don't just work on an individual entity. They actually start tracking an _entire graph of related entities_, putting them all to the `Added` state." saving/related-data.md: "the blog and three related posts are all inserted into the database. The posts are found and added, because they are reachable via the `Blog.Posts` navigation property." `Order.Items` is configured as such a navigation (`e.HasMany(o => o.Items).WithOne()` in DonHangDbContext), so AddAsync(order) stages every OrderItem.

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:db/schema.sql`: products, customers, orders, payments and notifications each declare `id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`; order_items declares no id and ends with `PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)`. The EF model agrees: InitialCreate annotates each of those five id columns with IdentityByDefaultColumn, and DonHangDbContext has `e.HasKey(i => new { i.OrderId, i.ProductId })` for OrderItem.

issues.text: "gets its own transaction" is one step stronger than the docs allow for the pinned version. saving/transactions.md: AutoTransactionBehavior.WhenNeeded "(default): EF creates a transaction only when needed. For example, most single SQL statements execute in a transaction implicitly, so EF doesn't create an explicit transaction." And when a transaction is already open on the context, SaveChanges "automatically creates a savepoint" rather than a transaction of its own. What is always true by default is the all-or-nothing scope per call, which is what the rest of the sentence needs.
issues.quote: By default, each `SaveChangesAsync()` call gets its own transaction: a later call cannot undo what an earlier one already saved.
issues.fix: Replace with: "By default, one `SaveChangesAsync()` call saves its staged changes all-or-nothing and independently of any other call: a later call cannot undo what an earlier one already saved." Update claim 9's text the same way, and the phrase "each `SaveChangesAsync()` call is its own transaction" in quiz q6's `correct` explanation (en + vi). Do not introduce AutoTransactionBehavior or savepoints in the body — out of scope per depth_notes.

issues.text: "every object it holds a reference to" drops both conditions the docs attach. explicit-tracking.md: the Add methods "actually start tracking an _entire graph of related entities_" — related, i.e. reached through navigation properties (related-data.md: "reachable via the `Blog.Posts` navigation property"), and the API contract adds "that are not already being tracked". As written, a reader can take it to cover any field an object references, and to re-mark an already-tracked item as `Added`.
